story920:
Apistotoke — called Ihtsipatapiyohpa, the Old Man Who Creates Us By Thought — stood in the void before creation. There was nothing around him. No ground beneath his feet, no sky above his head. Only the darkness and the silence and the power of his own mind.

He thought, and the thought became Sky Beings. Naato'si the Sun was the first — a being of fire and light who would illuminate everything that followed. Ko'komiki'somm the Moon was the second — a being of silver and shadow who would govern the night. And the stars came after, scattered across the sky like embers from a fire.

Then Apistotoke created Ksahkomitapi — the Earth — as mother to all creation. She was the ground beneath the sky, the body that held the roots, the foundation upon which all life would build.

Apistotoke then created Na'pi — Old Man — the first man and demigod who would shape the world with his own hands. Na'pi was not merely a human but a being of creative power, capable of molding the earth like clay and breathing life into the forms he made.

With his wife Kipitaakii — Old Lady — Na'pi set about the work of creation. They made the mountains and the valleys, the rivers and the lakes, the forests and the plains.

But the earth was covered in water. A great flood had washed over the land, and nothing grew. Na'pi sent Turtle to dive to the bottom of the flood and bring up mud. Turtle dove deep — deeper than any creature had gone before — and surfaced with a pawful of mud in his webbed hand.

Na'pi took the mud and shaped it. He molded it into hills and plains, into riverbeds and lake beds. He placed the mud on the back of a great turtle, and the mud grew, spreading across the shell until it became the land — Turtle Island, the Blackfoot call it.

Na'pi created men and women, animals and plants. He taught the Blackfoot people which plants to eat and which to avoid. He showed them which animals to hunt — especially the buffalo, whose body provided food, clothing, shelter, and tools.

When his work was done, Na'pi departed. He walked toward the western mountain and disappeared into the sunset. But his creation endures — the land, the people, the buffalo, the stars — all of it the thought of Apistotoke, shaped by the hands of Na'pi.
story921:
Na'pi discovered two bags in a lodge at the edge of the world. One bag was warm and bright, filled with the essence of summer — the heat of the sun, the green of the grass, the hum of insects. The other bag was cold and dark, filled with the essence of winter — the bite of frost, the silence of snow, the stillness of frozen rivers.

Na'pi was a practical being. He saw no reason why winter should be longer than summer, or summer longer than winter. "I will make them equal," he declared. He tried to steal both bags, but the bags were guarded by spirits who watched them day and night.

Na'pi sent a prairie chicken to steal the summer bag. The prairie chicken was small and quick, and it succeeded where Na'pi had failed — it grabbed the bag in its claws and flew away.

The guardians chased the bird across the plains. They caught up to it and sliced at the grass with their knives, cutting the bag open. Strong wind burst forth — the hot wind of summer that dries the rivers and cracks the earth.

The summer bag was ruined. Its contents scattered across the land in patches — here a warm day, there a cold snap, everywhere the remnants of a summer that had been torn apart.

Later, Na'pi burned himself on a fire. The pain was terrible, and he needed cooling wind to ease his suffering. He climbed a mountain and performed a medicine ceremony, calling the wind from the four directions. The wind came — but too strongly. It blew so fiercely that Na'pi was nearly thrown from the mountain.

He survived by grabbing a birch tree, wrapping his fingers around its trunk. His fingers left marks in the bark — the distinctive patterned marks that birch trees still bear today.

The story explains why seasons are unequal, why birch trees have patterned bark, and why the wind sometimes comes too strong. It is a Blackfoot teaching about the consequences of tampering with the natural order — and the persistence of the marks left by those who try.
story922:
After a great flood swept through the land, Na'pi gathered all the people on top of a large mountain. They were wet, frightened, and exhausted. They had lost everything — their homes, their stored food, their ceremonial objects. All they had was each other.

Na'pi looked at the people and said, "You must learn to live together. But first, you must learn to speak to each other."

He gave them water of different colors — black, red, yellow, and white — and told them to drink. Each person chose a color and drank.

Those who drank the black water spoke the same language — the language of the Piegan, the Siksika, and the Blood people. These were the bands of the Blackfoot Confederacy, bound together by a shared tongue and a shared memory of the flood.

Those who drank the red water spoke another language. Those who drank the yellow spoke another still. And those who drank the white spoke a language that sounded like wind through grass.

The people who spoke different languages could no longer understand each other. They drifted apart, forming separate tribes, separate nations, separate worlds. But the Blackfoot remained together, for they shared the black water and the black water's language.

The event was said to have taken place on the highest mountain in the Montana reservation — a peak so tall that the snow never fully melts and the wind never stops blowing. The Blackfoot still climb it sometimes, though not for the water. They climb to remember the time when all people spoke one language, and to honor the moment when that unity was broken.

The story teaches that diversity is not a punishment but a consequence of creation — that the world is made richer by the variety of voices, even as it is made more complex. And it teaches that the Blackfoot Confederacy is special — chosen not by favoritism but by the accident of which water they drank.
story923:
The Snake First Nations told the Blackfoot about a powerful medicine stone that lay in the valley between what is now McLeod and Fort Benton, Montana, near the Marias River. The stone was ancient and sacred, pulsing with spiritual energy that could heal the sick and protect the people.

Years passed. The Blackfoot remembered the story but did not act on it. Then a group of men decided to travel to find the stone. They were young and brave, and they believed that finding the stone would bring glory to their band.

When they discovered it, the leader laughed. He rolled the stone down the hill, mocking the story. "This is just a rock," he said. "The Snake people told us lies."

His companions were uneasy. They had heard the warnings about disrespecting sacred objects. But the leader was confident, and confidence is contagious.

On their return journey, they were ambushed in battle by enemies. The fight was fierce, and the Blackfoot were outnumbered. All but one man were killed. The survivor limped back to the village carrying the news of the disaster.

The place became known as Red Coulee — named for the blood that soaked the ground that day. And ever after, the Blackfoot would leave offerings when passing through the valley. They left tobacco, beads, and food — not because they feared the stone, but because they respected it.

The story teaches that sacred objects demand respect, and that mockery of spiritual power invites consequences. The leader who laughed at the stone did not die because the stone was evil, but because his disrespect opened him to the violence that the stone could have protected him from.
